subject: Cooking
title: Kefir: The Grain That Isn't a Grain
description: Learn Kefir: The Grain That Isn't a Grain in one minute.

hook.text: Kefir 'grains' look like tiny cauliflower florets. They're not grains at all — they're living microbial colonies.

buildup.text: Each grain contains over 60 species of bacteria and yeast bound together in a polysaccharide matrix.

discovery.text: Kefir grains originated in the Caucasus Mountains — shepherds discovered them growing in leather milk bags.

twist.text: Unlike yogurt, kefir contains yeast that produces small amounts of alcohol — typically 0.5–2%.

climax.text: Kefir has more diverse probiotics than any other fermented dairy product — up to 3x more than yogurt.

punchline.text: A living blob from the mountains makes the most probiotic drink on Earth.

quiz.question: What are kefir grains actually made of?
options: Living colonies of bacteria and yeast

details.summary: Kefir grains are gelatinous clusters of bacteria and yeast that ferment milk into a tangy, effervescent probiotic drink. Despite the name, they contain no cereal grain — the term describes their appearance. Kefir contains a far more diverse microbial community than yogurt.
details.whyItMatters: Kefir grains are a unique symbiotic culture passed down through generations. Their complex microbial diversity produces a probiotic drink with more beneficial strains than most fermented dairy.
takeaways: Kefir grains contain dozens of bacterial and yeast species together
The drink is naturally effervescent from CO2 produced by yeasts
Kefir offers more diverse probiotics than standard yogurt

faq.question: How are kefir grains different from yogurt starter?
faq.answer: Yogurt uses two to three bacterial strains. Kefir grains contain 30 to 50 species of bacteria and yeast in a polysaccharide matrix. The grains are self-perpetuating — they grow and can be divided indefinitely. Yogurt starter weakens over generations and needs refreshing.

faq.question: Where do kefir grains come from originally?
faq.answer: Kefir grains originated in the Caucasus Mountains region thousands of years ago. They cannot be created from scratch in a lab — new grains must come from existing ones. The exact origin remains a mystery, making them one of fermentation's enduring puzzles.
